title: Law Firm Tech Budgets Drive the Build Versus Buy AI Debate
author: Ethan Schenker

dom.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of vertical-vendor durability as contingent rather than assured and materially extends it with concrete law-firm strategies: proprietary workflows paired with interchangeable models, subscription products used as transitional bridges, and hybrid build-and-buy architectures. This strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on model portability and flexible sourcing as practical hedges against vendor and technology change.
qs: A chief innovation officer at another large law firm said that while the firm hadn’t built its own platform from scratch, lawyers have access to an internally built AI platform that integrates proprietary workflows and allows users to swap out large language models.

Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereyra said he sees a false choice that wrongly assumes “either firms are going to build everything themselves, or a company like us or a model provider is going to build everything themselves.”  For now, firms said they are evaluating their investment decisions through a similar lens, prioritizing flexibility to swap out their AI tools for the latest technology.

st.t: AI hiring: Implementation demand meets recruitment uncertainty
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s investment-allocation theme by showing that limited new-technology budgets constrain build-versus-buy choices and that proprietary development can coexist with external tools. It supports a conditional, hybrid strategy rather than establishing that internal development produces superior value or returns.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between AI access and dependable firm integration, and materially extends it by showing how limited new-technology budgets, proprietary-development plans, and hybrid build-versus-buy strategies shape implementation. It also reinforces the need to distinguish announced investment from completed expenditure or demonstrated returns.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The report materially develops the cluster’s scale-dependent account of AI differentiation and implementation. It provides spending data and executive evidence that the largest firms can absorb build-or-buy costs and influence vendors, while smaller firms generally rely on external tools. It does not establish that proprietary investment itself creates durable advantage, and some projected spending remains prospective.
qs: Big Law firms “have the scale to really absorb the cost of AI, whether that’s through build or buy,” Rusanow added.
With thousands of lawyers—and thousands of potential licenseholders—the biggest firms say they can also shape legal tech products before market.

It adds survey evidence and concrete firm plans showing investment in proprietary AI, scale and internal data, while also supporting the cluster’s nuanced build-versus-buy framing by noting that external tools may remain part of enterprise solutions. It does not address the cluster’s broader claims about bargaining shifts toward legal departments or ALSPs.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on institutional absorption and extends it with concrete budget evidence: Big Law spending remains concentrated on recurring technology, while major firms are pursuing proprietary platforms that leverage firm data but may still incorporate external tools. It therefore sharpens the practical build-versus-buy dimension without establishing broader service-model transformation or realised ROI.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by presenting build-versus-buy as a task-dependent portfolio choice shaped by cost, proprietary data, vendor capability and firm scale. It also reinforces the qualified conclusion that scale may advantage large firms, while its spending evidence and forecasts do not establish durable competitive superiority.

Big Law firms “have the scale to really absorb the cost of AI, whether that’s through build or buy,” Rusanow added.

kp.k: Large firms reported limited new-technology spending in 2025
kp.d: Bloomberg Law reports that roughly 67% of large firms spent under 2% of their 2025 budgets on building or buying new technology. Among firms with more than a thousand lawyers, 12 supplied additional survey data, and subscriptions and recurring technology costs far exceeded new-technology spending. Sixty-six firms of all sizes reported both categories. Firms classified their own spending, a stated qualification to the figures; the categories cover technology generally, not exclusively AI.
qs: Roughly 67% of large firms reported spending under 2% of their 2025 budgets on building or buying new technology, according to data shared with Bloomberg Law.

At firms with more than a thousand lawyers, 12 of which opted to share additional data for Bloomberg’s Leading Law Firms survey, outlays on technology subscriptions and recurring costs far eclipsed spending on new technology.
Sixty-six firms of all sizes reported spending in both categories.
Firms had the discretion to categorize their own technology spending in the survey.

kp.k: AI spending growth could redirect budgets toward internal development
kp.d: Citigroup law firm adviser Gretta Rusanow expects industrywide AI spending to accelerate steeply in 2026 and beyond. The article presents internal investment by leading firms as evidence of this direction, reporting Kirkland & Ellis’s announced $500 million proprietary AI model plans and DLA Piper’s enterprise approach using scale and proprietary data. These are plans and expectations, not completed investments or demonstrated returns; internal development could divert money otherwise available for subscriptions.
qs: There are signs the tide is turning, as industrywide spending on AI is expected to steeply accelerate in 2026 and beyond, said Gretta Rusanow, managing director and head of advisory services at Citigroup Inc.’s law firm group.
plans to pour $500 million into building a proprietary AI model
are looking to invest internally, steering money into developing their own tools and away from what could otherwise be spent on legal AI subscriptions.
DLA Piper is “moving towards an enterprise solution” that leverages scale and proprietary data, although outside AI tools will still likely play a role, said Loren Brown, the firm’s US vice chair.

kp.k: Flexible internal platforms can treat subscriptions as transitional
kp.d: An anonymous large-firm chief innovation officer reports that lawyers use an internally built platform incorporating proprietary workflows and interchangeable large language models, although the firm has not built its platform from scratch. This executive characterizes Harvey and Legora subscriptions as a bridge. More broadly, firms describe prioritizing the ability to replace AI tools as technology changes.
qs: A chief innovation officer at another large law firm said that while the firm hadn’t built its own platform from scratch, lawyers have access to an internally built AI platform that integrates proprietary workflows and allows users to swap out large language models.
For this firm, the subscription legal AI platforms like Harvey and Legora are “a bridge,” said the executive, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about law firm spending.
For now, firms said they are evaluating their investment decisions through a similar lens, prioritizing flexibility to swap out their AI tools for the latest technology.

kp.k: Ropes & Gray favors buying amid rapid technological change
kp.d: Management committee member Jane Rogers frames building versus buying as a business as well as a technology decision. Ropes & Gray has chosen to buy: CIO Marsha Stein argues that rapid technological change currently makes proprietary development unattractive and that technology companies can develop the technology better. This is the firm’s conditional strategic judgment, not a general finding that buying always outperforms building.
qs: The decision to build in-house or buy from legal technology companies is a business decision as much as a technology one, Rogers said. Ropes & Gray, for its part, has opted to buy.
“The technology is changing so quickly now that it doesn’t appear to us at this point that doing something proprietary makes sense,” said Ropes & Gray Chief Information Officer Marsha Stein.
“Right now, the best option, we think, is to actually buy.”
“We think that technology companies can do that better than we can do in a proprietary way.”

kp.k: Hybrid strategies challenge an exclusive build-or-buy choice
kp.d: Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereyra rejects the premise that either firms or vendors must build everything. DLA Piper’s Loren Brown describes a mixed strategy: reducing the number of tools, combining commercial and proprietary solutions in some cases, and building or buying entirely in others. The article argues that these allocation decisions will affect legal AI companies dependent on licensing revenue.
qs: The targets of firms’ new AI investments will also impact the future of the dominant AI legal tech companies that rely on licensing revenue.

Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereyra said he sees a false choice that wrongly assumes “either firms are going to build everything themselves, or a company like us or a model provider is going to build everything themselves.”

While DLA Piper expects to reduce the number of AI tools it relies on, Brown said that he sees the firm, in some cases, opting to “use commercial tools in addition to some proprietary solution,” while choosing to entirely build or buy in other scenarios, he said.

kp.k: Smaller firms face higher proportional costs and building constraints
kp.d: Nearly 30% of firms with fewer than 500 attorneys reported spending more than 5% of their 2025 budgets on new technology; 1 in 3 reported spending more than 8% on subscriptions and recurring costs. The article says smaller firms spent higher average budget shares on new technology but considers proprietary AI model investment unlikely without scale. Offit Kurman CIO Alex Finkel asserts that build-versus-buy is not an applicable choice beyond the top 50 firms; this categorical boundary is his view, rather than a survey finding.
qs: Beyond the top 50 firms, “the build-versus-buy selection or strategy is not applicable to anyone,” said Offit Kurman Chief Innovation Officer Alex Finkel.
Smaller firms, on average, spent higher shares of their budgets last year on new technology.
Nearly 30% of firms with fewer than 500 attorneys reported spending more than 5% of their budget on new technology last year.
Without the advantage of scale, these smaller firms’ investments are not likely going towards proprietary AI models.
Instead, 1 in 3 firms with fewer than 500 attorneys told Bloomberg Law that they spent more than 8% of their 2025 budgets on technology subscriptions and recurring costs.

kp.k: Scale supports market advantage and influence over vendors
kp.d: The article characterizes the resulting market as more segmented, with firms able to fund AI development positioned to extend their advantage even if they buy instead. Rusanow attributes this to large firms’ capacity to absorb AI costs under either strategy. Large firms also report influencing products before market through the scale of their potential licenseholder base; Stein cites Ropes & Gray’s size as a source of development input.
qs: The resulting legal market is more segmented, and puts firms with the money to build AI in a position to push their advantage further—even if they don’t choose to do so.
Big Law firms “have the scale to really absorb the cost of AI, whether that’s through build or buy,” Rusanow added.
With thousands of lawyers—and thousands of potential licenseholders—the biggest firms say they can also shape legal tech products before market.
“We have a lot of input into the development of these tools,” Stein said. “We’re a big firm.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source describes accelerating AI investment, competing build/buy/hybrid strategies, and a more segmented legal market in which large firms have greater investment options and influence over vendors.
pts.d: Gretta Rusanow predicts that industrywide AI spending will accelerate steeply in 2026 and beyond. Ethan Schenker reports that major firms are directing investment toward internal tools rather than spending all of those funds on legal-AI subscriptions, citing Kirkland & Ellis's announced $500 million proprietary-model investment and DLA Piper's enterprise strategy. Loren Brown says DLA Piper is moving toward an enterprise solution using scale and proprietary data, expects to reduce its number of AI tools, and anticipates combining commercial and proprietary tools in some cases. An anonymous large-firm chief innovation officer describes an internal platform with proprietary workflows and interchangeable models, characterizing Harvey and Legora subscriptions as transitional. By contrast, Ropes & Gray has chosen to buy: Marsha Stein says rapid technological change currently makes proprietary development unattractive and that technology companies can develop the technology better. Harvey co-founder Gabriel Pereyra rejects an all-or-nothing choice between firms and vendors building everything. Alex Finkel contends that proprietary development is effectively unavailable outside the top 50 firms. Schenker concludes that the resulting market is more segmented and that firms able to afford internal AI development can extend their advantage even if they buy instead. Rusanow attributes that flexibility to scale, while Stein says large firms can influence product development.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines self-reported 2025 technology-budget data, announced investments, and interviewees' accounts of firm strategies; its forward-looking claims rest on those examples and professional judgments.
pts.d: Bloomberg Law's Leading Law Firms survey supplies descriptive spending evidence: 66 firms reported both new-technology spending and subscriptions/recurring costs, including 12 firms with more than 1,000 lawyers sharing additional data. Roughly 67% of large firms reported allocating under 2% of their 2025 budgets to new technology; nearly 30% of firms with fewer than 500 lawyers allocated more than 5%; and one-third of firms in that smaller-firm group allocated more than 8% to subscriptions and recurring costs. These are technology-budget categories, not separately measured AI expenditures, and firms categorized their own spending. Kirkland & Ellis's announced investment and accounts from DLA Piper, Ropes & Gray, and an anonymous innovation officer illustrate investment strategies rather than demonstrated outcomes. Rusanow's acceleration forecast, Finkel's top-50 threshold, and claims about scale advantages are attributed judgments; the article supplies no quantified forecast model or measured competitive effects. Bloomberg Law discloses that it is itself a legal technology provider.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Budget findings concern 2025; the spending forecast concerns 2026 onward; firm strategies are provisional and depend on technological change, scale, cost, and flexibility.
pts.d: The 2026 article uses 2025 spending as its historical baseline and places the build-versus-buy debate in the period since ChatGPT's market impact in 2022. Rusanow's forecast explicitly concerns 2026 and beyond. Kirkland & Ellis's investment is an announced plan, not a reported completed expenditure. Ropes & Gray's preference for buying is explicitly qualified as its current assessment amid fast-changing technology. DLA Piper's prospective reduction in tool numbers does not imply eliminating vendors: Brown anticipates different build, buy, and combined choices in different scenarios. Firms prioritize the ability to change tools and models as technology evolves. The anonymous executive's description of subscriptions as a bridge supplies no transition deadline. Finkel's feasibility claim is conditioned on firm size, and Schenker qualifies smaller firms' lack of proprietary-model investment as likely rather than certain.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern large firms, smaller firms, their lawyers, and legal-AI software vendors, with unequal capacity to fund development, absorb costs, and shape products.
pts.d: The largest firms gain a wider choice of internal development, commercial purchasing, and hybrid arrangements, supported by scale, proprietary data, and large potential license volumes. Smaller firms and boutiques are described as allocating larger budget shares to new technology while relying more on external expertise; proprietary-model development is generally portrayed as beyond their resources. Lawyers at the anonymous large firm have access to an internally built platform integrating proprietary workflows and interchangeable language models. Legal-AI vendors such as Harvey and Legora face potential changes in licensing demand as firms redirect investment internally, though hybrid strategies preserve a role for commercial tools. Stein says large purchasers influence tools before market release. The article does not establish effects on lawyer employment, legal-service quality, client fees, or public access to justice.
